# Data frame {#sec-dataframe}

{{< include ../preamble.qmd >}}

::: {style="margin-top: 1em; font-size: 125%; font-weight: 1000; text-align: center;"}
Tableau pratique
:::

The previous chapters introduced mathematical concepts in programming, such as vectors, matrices, logical and numeric values, and matrix operations. This chapter transitions from strict mathematical structures to the more flexible requirements of data science. The data frame was developed to meet these needs, and most data encountered in ecological practice are stored in this format.

A data frame stores multiple variables recorded across multiple observations.
For instance, an investigator surveys 100 individuals and records name, age, and sex. The dataset consists of three columns: the first for name as character, the second for age as integer, and the third as logical (TRUE if female and FALSE if male). Similarly, a field researcher visits fifteen sites and records site name, altitude, pH, and other variables.

A data frame is a rectangular structure (similar to a matrix @sec-matrixMath and @sec-matrixCoding), where each column represents a variable. However, unlike a matrix, the data type of each column can differ.

Another practical advantage of a data frame is that columns typically have names, allowing access by column name rather than numerical index.

## Formal {.unnumbered}

A data frame is constructed with the function `data.frame()`{.r}.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

# Construct a data frame where each argument defines a column name and its vector of values
df <- data.frame(
  name1 = vector1, # First column named name1
  name2 = vector2, # Second column named name2
  name3 = vector3  # Third column named name3
)
```

The constraint is that all vectors must have equal lengths; otherwise, the structure will not form a rectangle and the operation will fail.

Columns can be conveniently accessed using `df$name1`{.r}, which is the most common approach. Due to underlying data structures, this is equivalent to `df[, 1]`{.r} or `df["name1"]`{.r}.

## Examples {.unnumbered}

Below are three styles for creating a data frame. The third approach represents standard best practice.


```{r}
#| echo: true


# Method 1: Data frame created without specifying column names, resulting in default, uninformative names
my_df <- data.frame(
  c(1, 2, 3),
  c("A", "X", "B"),
  c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE))
my_df

# Method 2: Data frame created using existing vector names as column names
col1 <- c(1, 2, 3)
col2 <- c("A", "X", "B")
col3 <- c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE)

my_df <- data.frame(col1, col2, col3)
my_df

# Method 3: Data frame created with explicit, descriptive variable names
my_df <- data.frame(
  id = col1,
  letter = col2,
  male = col3)
my_df
```


- Different manners to extract column. The first approach represents standard best practice but can only extract one column. The remaning approach allows to extract more columns^[With dplyr, selecting columns is done with the function select]

```{r}
#| echo: true

# Extract a column using the dollar sign ($) operator (returns a vector)
my_df$id

# Extract the first column using matrix-style numerical indexing (returns a vector)
my_df[, 1]

# Subset a column by name using single brackets (returns a 1-column data frame)
my_df["id"]

# Extract a column by name using matrix-style character indexing (returns a vector)
my_df[, "id"]

# Extract two column by name using matrix-style character indexing (returns a 2-column data frame)
my_df[, c("id", "letter")]

```

- Appending a new column to a data frame

```{r}
#| echo: true

# Add a new column (variable) to the data frame
my_df$name <- c("Andry", "Feno", "Felana")
my_df
```

## Tips and warnings {.unnumbered}

- Column names are considered variables and should not include spaces or special characters; the same rules apply as in @sec-assignment.

- In principle, all input vectors when constructing a data frame should be of equal length. There is a special case where a vector of length one is provided: R creates a constant vector matching the length of the longest vector.

```{r}
#| echo: true

# Construct a data frame using a scalar (recycled) and a multi-element vector
data.frame(constant = 1, letters = c("A", "B", "C"))

```

- A `tibble`{.r} is a common variation of the data frame structure. The popular package ecosystem `tidyverse`{.r} prefers data formatted as a tibble, but standard data frames also work. The differences are subtle enough that either format can be used in most workflows.

- The basic concepts above are useful for understanding the core structure and goals of this volume. However, manual entry is not the ideal method for entering data into R. Most often, data are entered in spreadsheet software such as Excel and subsequently imported into R as a data frame.
